x.t: A new bridge crosses the Ganga river in Bihar
b: India has a new [[bridge|bridge]] over the [[ganga|Ganga]] river. It is called Nitish Setu. Prime Minister Narendra Modi opened it on Saturday.
The Ganga splits the state of [[bihar|Bihar]] into two parts. The new bridge joins the south and the north.
The bridge is nearly 10 kilometres long. It has six [[lane|lanes]]. That means six lines of cars and trucks fit across it.

o.t: Nitish Setu, a six-lane bridge over the Ganga, opens in Bihar
b: Prime Minister Narendra Modi opened Nitish Setu, a new [[bridge|bridge]] over the [[ganga|River Ganga]], on Saturday 21 November. A bridge is a structure built over something, such as a river, so that people or vehicles can get across. Nitish Setu links Kachchi Dargah in Patna district with Bidupur in Vaishali district.
The Ganga naturally divides the state of [[bihar|Bihar]] into two regions, the north and the south. Nitish Setu crosses the river to join the two.

The main bridge is nearly 10 kilometres long. Together with its approach roads, the roads that lead up to each end, the whole project is about 20 kilometres long. The bridge has six [[lane|lanes]]. A lane is a part of a road, marked by painted lines, for a single line of vehicles.

stories.think: A big river can split a place into two parts. How do you think people crossed wide rivers before there were bridges?

quiz.q: Which river does Nitish Setu cross?

x.t: Bumblebees have small brains but can do clever things
b: [[bumblebee|Bumblebees]] have very small brains. But they can do clever things. Two scientists describe this in a science [[journal|journal]].
They looked at earlier tests on bees. Bumblebees can solve new problems. They can learn hard tasks by watching other bees. They can even pass mood-like feelings to other bees in their nest.
Next, scientists want to compare maps of insect brains. That could show how bees do so much.

o.t: Scientists review what bumblebees can do with small brains
b: Two scientists have described the clever things [[bumblebee|bumblebees]] can do with very small brains. Lars Chittka, of Queen Mary University of London, and Stanley Heinze, of Lund University, wrote a Perspective in the [[journal|journal]] Science on 19 November. A journal is a magazine about one subject. A Perspective is a kind of review: it brings together earlier research instead of reporting a new experiment.

The research they describe shows that bumblebees can solve problems they have never met before. They can learn difficult tasks just by watching other bees. They can even pass on emotion-like states, a little like moods, to their nestmates, the other bees in their nest.

What comes next? The scientists suggest comparing connectomes, which are detailed maps of the connections inside a brain, across different insects. This could help show which brain wiring makes clever behaviour possible.

stories.think: Have you ever learned something just by watching someone else do it? What was it, and how did watching help?

quiz.q: How can bumblebees learn difficult tasks?

x.t: India move ahead of New Zealand in the first Test
b: India are playing New Zealand in a long cricket match called a Test. It is at the [[basin-reserve|Basin Reserve]] in Wellington, New Zealand.
[[kl-rahul|KL Rahul]] scored 136 runs. It was his 13th Test [[century|century]]. To make a century, a player must score 100 runs. Shubman Gill was out for 98, just two short.
India have 486 runs. New Zealand made 368. So India are 118 runs ahead.

o.t: Rahul hits a century as India lead New Zealand by 118
b: India ended day three of the first Test against New Zealand on Saturday on 486 for 4, meaning four batters were out. The match is at the [[basin-reserve|Basin Reserve]] in Wellington. New Zealand scored 368 in their first [[innings|innings]], a team's turn to bat. India have passed that total, so they lead by 118 runs.

[[kl-rahul|KL Rahul]] scored 136, his 13th Test [[century|century]]. A century is a score of 100 runs by one player. Rahul and Devdutt Padikkal, who made 80, added 165 runs together. Shubman Gill was [[bowled|bowled]] by Jacob Duffy for 98, just two runs short of a century. Bowled means the ball hit his wicket, so he was out.
Rishabh Pant is 55 not out, meaning he is still batting. On day four, India will try to make their lead bigger, while New Zealand will hope to get India's batters out.

stories.think: Shubman Gill was out just two runs short of 100. How do you think a player feels after coming so close, and what could a friend say to cheer them up?

quiz.q: How many runs did KL Rahul score?

x.t: India's first IIT turns 75 and gets a special coin
b: [[iit-kharagpur|IIT Kharagpur]] is India's first IIT. IIT stands for Indian Institute of Technology. It is a kind of university. This year it is celebrating 75 years.
Long ago, the place was a camp where freedom fighters were held. They wanted India to be free from British rule.
On Saturday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited. He showed a special [[coin|coin]] made for the 75 years. He also met students.

o.t: IIT Kharagpur, India's first IIT, celebrates 75 years with a coin
b: [[iit-kharagpur|IIT Kharagpur]], the first Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) in the country, is celebrating 75 years. This celebration is called its Platinum [[jubilee|Jubilee]]. A jubilee is a special anniversary of an event, and the celebrations connected with it. The institute is in Kharagpur, a city in West Bengal.

The campus has a long history. It stands on a site that was once a detention camp, a place where people were held. During British rule, freedom fighters, people who struggled for India's freedom, were held there.

On Saturday 21 November, Prime Minister Narendra Modi unveiled a commemorative [[coin|coin]] marking the institute's 75 years. To unveil something means to show it to the public for the first time. A commemorative coin is made to honour a special event. He also met students at the institute as part of the Platinum Jubilee celebrations.

stories.think: IIT Kharagpur stands where freedom fighters were once held. Why do you think it matters to remember the history of a place?

quiz.q: What did Prime Minister Modi unveil at IIT Kharagpur?

x.t: Two new tiny water bears found on an underwater mountain
b: Scientists have found two new kinds of [[tardigrade|water bear]]. Water bears are tiny animals with eight short, thick legs. You need a microscope to see them.
The new ones live on an [[seamount|underwater mountain]] near [[cape-verde|Cape Verde]], off West Africa.
The top of the mountain had 20 types of water bear. A much deeper place farther away had only two. Underwater mountains may be busy homes for tiny life.

o.t: Two new species of water bear found on an Atlantic seamount
b: Scientists have announced two new species, or kinds, of [[tardigrade|tardigrade]], also called water bears. Tardigrades are microscopic animals with four pairs of stout legs. The new species are named Megastygarctides hekatae and Parastygarctus potercha. The first is just under 0.2 millimetres long, and the second is about 0.07 millimetres.

They were found on Senghor Seamount, a [[seamount|seamount]] or underwater mountain off [[cape-verde|Cape Verde]], an island country of West Africa. The seafloor samples were collected in 2009 on the research ship Meteor, from the seamount's top, more than 100 metres down.

On the top, the team found 20 types of tardigrade. At a deep-sea site about 100 kilometres north, nearly 3,300 metres down, they found just two. The scientists say this supports the idea that seamounts are hotspots, places packed with life, for tardigrades in the sea.

stories.think: These tiny animals were only named this year. Why do you think there are still animals that no one has named?

quiz.q: Where were the two new water bears found?

x.t: Fastest driver gets a penalty, so Verstappen starts first
b: Formula 1 drivers raced against the clock in Las Vegas, in the United States. [[kimi-antonelli|Kimi Antonelli]] was the fastest.
But his team has used more engine parts than the rules allow this season. So he got a [[penalty|penalty]]. He must start five places back, in sixth.
Now [[max-verstappen|Max Verstappen]] starts at the front, in [[pole-position|pole position]]. George Russell starts second. The race comes next.

o.t: Verstappen on pole in Las Vegas after Antonelli's penalty
b: [[kimi-antonelli|Kimi Antonelli]] of Mercedes set the fastest time in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix in the United States. Qualifying is a timed session that decides where each car starts the race. Normally, the fastest driver earns [[pole-position|pole position]], the leading place at the start.

However, Antonelli has a five-place [[grid|grid]] [[penalty|penalty]]. The grid is the pattern of lines on the track that marks each car's starting spot. A penalty is a disadvantage given for breaking a rule. Formula 1 rules limit how many engine parts can be used in a season, and Antonelli's team has gone over that limit. So he drops from first to sixth.
That means [[max-verstappen|Max Verstappen]] of Red Bull, who was second fastest, starts on pole. George Russell starts second. The race comes next, with Verstappen at the front.

stories.think: Why do you think Formula 1 limits how many engine parts a team can use in a season?

quiz.q: Where will Kimi Antonelli start the race after his penalty?

bigStory.t: How far is one light-day from home?
bigStory.sub: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, reached one light-day from Earth on Wednesday

x.why: A spacecraft that left Earth in 1977 is still travelling. This week it got so far away that light needs a whole day to reach it.

o.why: A spacecraft launched in 1977 is still travelling, and its team on Earth still talks to it. This week it reached a distance so great that a radio signal, moving at the speed of light, needs 24 hours to get there.

facts: about one light-day: how far light travels in 24 hours
how long a radio signal from Earth now takes to reach it
the day it reached one light-day

days.o: NASA launched Voyager 1 on 5 September 1977. It flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, and in 1990 it took a picture of Earth known as the Pale Blue Dot. In 2012 it entered interstellar space, the space between the stars. It is run from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California.
days.x: Voyager 1 is a spacecraft. It left Earth in 1977. It flew past the planets Jupiter and Saturn. In 1990 it took a picture of Earth from very far away.

days.o: A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, about 25.9 billion kilometres. Light reaches the Moon in about 1.3 seconds, and sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. After sunset today, Tuesday 17 November, NASA invites people to flash VGR, Voyager's three-letter call sign, in Morse code towards the sky with a torch.
days.x: A light-day is how far light travels in one day. Sunlight reaches us in about 8 minutes. After sunset today, people can flash a torch for Voyager. Ask a grown-up to help.

days.o: NASA worked out that Voyager 1 would reach one light-day from Earth on Wednesday 18 November. No spacecraft has travelled this far before. A radio signal now takes about 24 hours to reach it, and its reply takes another day to come back. Voyager 2 is expected to reach one light-day in 2035.
days.x: On Wednesday, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. No spacecraft has gone this far before. A message now takes about a day to get there.

days.o: NASA talks to Voyager 1 by radio through its Deep Space Network, a set of giant radio antennas at three sites: Goldstone in California, near Madrid in Spain and near Canberra in Australia. The sites are placed around the world so that they can keep in contact with a spacecraft as Earth turns. Each site has one antenna that is 70 metres across. A radio signal now takes about 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and its reply takes another 24 hours to come back, so a message and its answer make a two-day round trip.
days.x: NASA talks to Voyager 1 with radio signals. It uses giant radio antennas in California, Spain and Australia. A message takes about a day to reach Voyager 1. The reply takes another day to come back.

days.o: On Wednesday 18 November Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. Its power source makes about 4 watts less every year, so NASA has been switching off instruments to save power. Even after it falls silent, it will keep travelling. It will take about 300 years to reach the inner edge of a distant region called the Oort Cloud. In about 40,000 years it is expected to pass another star. It carries a Golden Record with sounds, music and images from Earth, and greetings in 55 languages. On 14 November, NASA found that Voyager 1's signal was reaching Earth without its usual science data. NASA thinks the problem is in the onboard computer that collects the data, and engineers are working on it.
days.x: On Wednesday, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. Its power gets a little weaker every year. Even when it falls silent, it will keep travelling. It carries a Golden Record with sounds, music and pictures from Earth. As of 19 November, Voyager 1's messages were arriving without their science data. Engineers are working on the problem.

x.q: What gives a cyclone its power?

o.t: Why a cyclone grows weaker over land
b: Cyclones are storms that need warm ocean water to keep going. Cyclone Akvan grew weaker after it crossed the coast of Odisha on Friday 20 November. Here is why that happens to cyclones.

Warm ocean water is the storm's fuel. It gives the storm heat and moisture. When a cyclone moves over land, that supply is cut off, so the storm weakens quickly. Without the heat and moisture, it is harder for the storm to make the thunderstorms that keep it going.

Some people believe a cyclone weakens over land because of friction, or rubbing, against the ground. Weather agencies say that is not the main reason. The main reason is the loss of heat and moisture from the sea. Cyclones also weaken when they pass over cold water.
o.remember: Warm ocean water is a cyclone's fuel. Over land the storm loses that supply of heat and moisture, so it weakens.
o.q: What is the main reason a cyclone weakens when it moves over land?
a: It loses heat and moisture from the sea

backThen.t: People fly free in a hot-air balloon for the first time
backThen.o: On 21 November 1783, two men became the first people to make a free flight in a hot-air balloon, a flight in a balloon that was not tied to the ground. They were Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and François Laurent, the marquis d'Arlandes. They took off from the grounds of the Château de la Muette in Paris and flew for about 25 minutes. The balloon was made by the brothers Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier. Earlier, on 19 September 1783, the brothers had sent a sheep, a duck and a rooster up in a balloon at Versailles, in front of the royal family. The animals landed safely.
backThen.x: On this day in 1783, two men took off from Paris in a hot-air balloon. The balloon was not tied to the ground. They flew for about 25 minutes.
backThen.why: It was the first time people flew free of the ground.

hiddenWords.o: Tardigrade comes from the Latin word tardigradus, which means slow-paced. It is made from tardus, which means slow, and gradi, which means to walk or step.
Record comes from the Latin word recordari, which means to recall or remember. Recordari is built on cor, the Latin word for heart.
Orbit comes from the Latin word orbita, which means a track or rut.
